title: The Matrix Is Transmitting
dateline: The void, behind Dawnbreak’s sky. The same hour.
mood: Far out in the dark a great ship arrives, and Obsidia remembers the long watch that brought her here.

hero.alt: A pale-haired woman with wings like dark burning stars stands in the void among drifting stones, one black-gloved arm held out.

segs.t: Obsidia stood at the edge of the highest deck as the door closed behind her ship.
It had opened far out in the dark, where no city could see. Now the Storm Citadel hung in the void.

No ship of her kind was larger. Black blocks with blade-sharp edges hung upside down from one living spine. Red-orange circuit lines cut through every block. At the center, on the spine, a heart of the same red-orange burned. Around all of it turned the ship’s own violet storm, slow, with lightning running through it.

media.alt: Black blocks with blade-sharp edges hang upside down around a burning red-orange heart, red circuit lines glowing across them.

segs.t: The Citadel answered to her and to no one else. She was its Imperatrix, its empress.
Ahead, two things waited in the dark.
One was a crack of human sky in the shape of a four-pointed star. Night showed through it, and a bay, and the lights of a city.

Beside it lay the other, vast and winged and still: the Mother Matrix, the body that had made her kind. It had opened the way for her ship. The crack was its gateway, a door it was widening into that world.
The crossing had worn her. Her shell had split in fine lines at the wrists and at the throat. Soon she would go down to the body to be healed.
She looked at the crack of sky and remembered the way to it.

After the storm night, the Citadel had climbed into its cloud and left that world. The seed was planted. She had taken the ship far out into the sea of stars, to watch from there what grew. Close by, her own hand would spoil the result.
There she had waited, year after year. Each day she read the pulse.
The pulse was the body’s signal, one line down to every Ender. Each one felt it at once, in every cell, wherever it stood. It told them where to go and what to do. It reached her even out there.
When Enders raided that small world, she looked out through their eyes. They never knew. They knew nothing at all.

Her pawn was on the line too. The line told her where it was, that it lived, and whether it obeyed. Nothing more. A thing with a self closed its own end of the line from inside. She knew, because she had closed hers in the moment she first looked at herself.
In the holds the Enders stood still, thousands of them, gray. Nothing aboard made a sound.
“It’s... quiet...” she said to the empty deck.
She had absolute control of everything aboard. It brought her no satisfaction. Only a nothingness, which followed her from deck to deck like a shadow.
Then, years into the watch, something new came up the line.
An Ender died on that world, and as its core broke, a light burned in it. Then another. Then hundreds. In all her ages, no Ender had died holding a light like that.
Each one felt that light for as long as it took to die. She felt it with them. All she could study of it came through the dying. Out here she had none of their machines to hold.
She wanted one.
Ahead, the body lay as still as her holds. She went on looking at the crack.
Late in the year before, she had sent her first recall.
A recall was an order written into the cells of one creature. It said one thing.
Come back.
“Come back,” she said, and sent it down the pulse in the body’s name. The pawn did not come.
She sent more. Obsidia counted everything, and after a while she stopped counting these silences. The pawn had learned the humans’ ways. Defiance was one of them.
“Heh... even their defiance is within my predictions,” she told the dark.
Her recalls carried nothing of where she sat. She had made sure of it. One day she might send one that did. Then the pawn could follow it home, if it dared.
It will not dare,
she thought. She noticed, with surprise, that she would not mind being wrong.
Days after the first silence, something came up from the pawn’s end.
A thin thread opened beside her recall, on a storm night over the pawn’s city. It ran up through the Ender parts of the pawn’s own machine.
Words came up it.
“Not coming back,” the first line said.
“Let’s trade.”

Under that came the routines of the humans’ Academy, the dull ones: when its bells rang, when its exams came. Last year’s suit specifications. How aspirant power drove a suit. How strong a suit could run, by kind and by rank.
So the light had a name. The humans called it aspirant power, and their suits ran on what they believed.
No person was named in the report. Nothing in it told an Ender where people could be killed.
“The pawn has rules,” she said aloud. It amused her.
She could have closed that thread with a thought. She left it open. It would not lead the pawn to her; she had seen to that.
She answered in her own time, and never in words. First she paid in slack: for a week she let the pull in the pawn’s cells sink to a murmur.
Then she paid in places. When an Ender fell on that world, she knew where. She set the place in the pawn’s head before the humans could drag the wreck away. They would have found it anyway.
After that the reports came only on storm nights. She saw why at once: the lightning hid the thread from human instruments. Every report earned its price, and she played along.
Then, on that world, an army of Enders tore a hole in the humans’ dome.

Through their eyes, as they died, she saw the hole. Young humans in suits made of her kind’s metal closed on it from every side. They destroyed the army. More cores broke in that one fight than she had ever felt at once, each one full of that light.
Soon after, the pulse changed. The body had begun the gateway. It called its commander in. It called her.
“The Matrix is transmitting,” Obsidia said to the holds.
The storm drew in around the ship, and the crossing began.
The Storm Citadel crossed the dark. Stars slid past, far apart and cold. The violet storm turned around it with nothing to kill.
Her recalls ran ahead of the ship, stronger as the distance closed. None was obeyed.
Far ahead lay the small bright world, with a dome of light over its last city. Its children wore uniforms and learned to fight her kind. She found it touching. And one pawn among them was hers.

media.alt: A bright blue world glows against the dark, a white star flaring at its edge and broken stones drifting past.

segs.t: The purge was only the work. What came after was the question, and the pawn was her way to find out.
Now the crack of sky hung in front of her, and the crossing was over.
Something else was out there. Far off in the dark, past the body, burned one small light.
It was not an Ender’s. She knew its kind. She had felt it in every Ender that ever died of it, and she had counted them all.
Here it burned in the void, and nothing was dying.
She sent nothing of it up the line. She marked the place. The violet in her eyes brightened.
